title: Stop Calling It Feedback
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Argues the word 'feedback' itself carries an implicit power claim that triggers resistance, since it frames a message as a directive from someone with authority rather than an option. Walks through a sliding scale of framing -- feedback, advice, recommendation, suggestion -- showing that each step down in perceived power lowers resistance and raises the odds a message gets acted on, using the same identical content throughout. Notes that a suggestion also implicitly points to the future, making it harder to respond to defensively than a statement about something already done. Concludes leaders should largely retire 'feedback' in favor of 'suggestion' or 'recommendation,' reserving actual feedback for moments requiring formal directive weight, such as performance reviews.
points: The word 'feedback' carries an implicit power claim that triggers resistance, even when the underlying message is identical to a softer framing.
Reframing the same content as 'advice,' 'recommendation,' or 'suggestion' lowers perceived power and measurably raises the odds it gets acted on.
A recommendation is inherently future-oriented, making it harder for the recipient to respond defensively than a statement about something already done.
quotes: When we call a message “feedback,” we do so because it comes from a place of power, status, or authority.
Leaders who give others “feedback” expect those receiving it to take it seriously and to act on it. It is not offered as an option. It is presented as a directive.
Whenever leaders depend on authority, position, status, or power to convey a message, it produces the visceral reaction of resistance. Ironically, this makes the message less likely to be acted on.
The reduction in power lowers resistance and increases the odds that the message will be taken up and acted on. All because of a word choice.
Equally important is the fact that a recommendation is about the future. It is difficult to respond negatively or defensively to something that hasn’t happened yet.
In fact, we might go as far as to say that leaders should get out of the feedback business and get into the recommendation and suggestion business—permanently.
